frase_gancho.texto: A yarn headdress whose colors tell whether a woman is single or married.

puente_narrativo.texto: We leave the Huasteca and travel south, to the highlands of Chiapas. Look for a thick, dark wool garment without sleeves, like a short tunic, made by weavers from San Juan Chamula.

guion_corto.texto: The petob is the headdress of Teenek women, or Huastec women, of San Luis Potosí. In the Teenek language, the word can name something round, like a coil. It is made with skeins of colored yarn. They are braided with the hair, from the nape of the neck to the forehead, and form a kind of crown on the head. The colors give information about the woman who wears it. A single woman wears only green and pink, a married woman adds red and orange, and a widow may choose whichever she likes. In the past it was made with plant fibers and cotton, and after the conquest wool was added. It is the complement of the embroidered quechquémitl you saw at the beginning of this hall, and together the two make up the formal dress.

guion_largo.texto:
A quechquémitl is worn over the shoulders, and a hat is placed on top of the head. The petob is neither one nor the other, because it is woven into the hair. When a Teenek woman gets ready for a celebration, she braids skeins of yarn with her own hair. She does it from the nape of the neck to the forehead, until hairstyle and headdress become one and the same.

The word comes from the Teenek language. Linguistic studies of the Huasteca explain that the term refers to something round, a coil. It is a good description, because the yarn forms a thick ring around the head, like a halo of colors. Remember that Teenek belongs to the Maya family of languages, although the people who speak it live far from Yucatán and Chiapas.

The materials have changed over time. That same study explains that in the past the headdress was made with vine fibers and cotton. After the arrival of the Spanish, wool began to be used. In recent decades, acrylic yarn, which is a synthetic fiber, has become common. The thread changes, but the shape and the gesture of braiding it remain the same.

The most interesting part is the colors, because they work like a language. The colors usually mentioned are pink, orange, green, yellow, and red. According to texts about the Huasteca of San Luis Potosí, a single woman wears only green and pink. When she marries, red and orange are added. If she is widowed, she may use whichever colors she likes. Someone who knows the code can read a woman’s status just by looking at her head. It is a writing made of wool, without letters, that can be read at a glance in the plaza, at the market, or at a celebration.

It is not the only garment that speaks this way. A text on Teenek handicrafts says that a quechquémitl without fringes indicates that the woman is single. If that is true, head and shoulders tell the same story, each in its own way.

What does the round shape mean? There is no definitive answer. One researcher proposes linking it with Mother Earth, with the moon, and with fertility. His idea is that the headdress blends fibers with hair, and that hair is associated with the threads of the loom and with rain. He himself warns that this is hard to affirm, because almost no images of headdresses from the pre-Hispanic era survive. For that reason it is best to take it as an idea and not as a fact.

Now think about everything a Teenek woman wears when she is dressed up. There is a language from the Maya family and a cross-stitch embroidery with the four-petaled flower. And there is a color code on the head. It is a way of wearing identity, without needing to say a word.

Before moving on, go back in memory to the first piece in this hall. The quechquémitl and the petob were made to go together, one over the shoulders and the other over the hair. And if you see red and orange among the green and pink, you already know something about the woman who wore it.

texto: Count the colors of the yarn and name them one by one
Look to see whether there is only green and pink, or also red and orange
Notice the round shape that surrounds the head, like a ring

texto.Material: Skeins of colored yarn braided with the hair (formerly plant fibers and cotton; later, wool)
texto.Origin: Huasteca of San Luis Potosí, San Luis Potosí

texto.pregunta: Myth: The headdresses of Indigenous women are just decoration.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The petob works as a code: its colors indicate whether the woman who wears it is single, married, or widowed.
